questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: The most expensive restaurants in Bangkok
Stews and soups that are kept cooking for years
How to cook camel and caiman
Why old food is dangerous to eat
questions.why: They discuss 'forever food' – dishes kept going day after day, year after year.

questions.q: What unusual foods have Beth and Phil eaten?
options: Both of them enjoyed eating camel
Phil didn't like caiman at all, but Beth loved camel
Beth didn't enjoy camel, but Phil loved caiman
Neither of them has eaten anything unusual
questions.why: Beth ate camel and didn't like it; Phil ate caiman and it was delicious.

questions.q: What did listener David Shirley discover in Bangkok?
options: A restaurant that serves only vegetables
A soup made from 50 different ingredients from the market
A cook who is 50 years old
A stew that had been cooking for fifty years
questions.why: He says he found a stew that had been simmering for fifty years.

questions.q: How is a perpetual stew kept going?
options: The pot is never emptied; new ingredients and water are added
It is frozen and heated again each day
It is cooked once a year for a festival
It is emptied and started again with fresh ingredients every week
questions.why: Phil says the pot is never completely emptied; new ingredients and water are added.

questions.q: What does writer Fuchsia Dunlop say about the Chinese '100-year-old broth'?
options: She isn't sure it's strictly true, but thinks it's possible
She has tasted it many times
She says it's definitely a myth
She thinks it's too dangerous to eat because of the risk of illness
questions.why: She says she doesn't know if it's strictly true, but 'theoretically' it's possible.

questions.q: According to Fuchsia, what do cooks need to do to keep the broth safe?
options: Add lots of chilli
Keep it in a cold place
Change the pot every month and wash it carefully with soap
Skim it, boil it every day and keep adding more
questions.why: She says you always skim it, boil it every day and replenish it as needed.

questions.q: According to historian Martha Carlin, why might medieval people keep a stew bubbling?
options: Because meat was very cheap
Starting a fire was hard, and they'd always have a hot meal ready
Because keeping a pot on the fire was an important religious tradition
Because they didn't like fresh food
questions.why: She says starting a fire was cumbersome, and keeping the pot going meant a hot meal was always waiting.

questions.q: What does Phil add about keeping a fire going all day in the Middle Ages?
options: Everyone did it
It was against the law
Only rich families could afford enough wood
It was only done in winter when it was very cold
questions.why: He says only rich families were able to afford enough wood to keep a fire going all day.
